result: The fly proboscis is a multifunctional segmented appendage homologous to a limb that extends during feeding, courtship, grooming, flight-associated respiration, and wing expansion after eclosion, and is capable of directed reaching towards food targets using gustatory information from leg taste receptors.
evaluation: Claims C1-C7 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Bridges and Dobzhansky 1933; Dethier 1976; Sturtevant 1915; Szebenyi 1969; Lehmann and Heymann 2005; Baker and Truman 2002). The multifunctionality claim (C7) is a reasonable inference from the documented diverse contexts of proboscis extension.

result: A collection of split GAL4 fly strains was created using the split GAL4 technique to identify and separately target the primary motor neurons for every proboscis muscle, building on previous work that identified some critical motor neurons using broader GAL4 lines or stochastic techniques.
evaluation: Claims C8-C11 are well-supported. C8-C10 cite appropriate prior work establishing the context (Baek and Mann 2009; O'Sullivan et al. 2018; Gordon and Scott 2009; Schwarz et al. 2017; Luan et al. 2006). C11 describes the main methodological contribution of this study, which is documented throughout the manuscript with detailed tables and figures.

result: Eight of the 16 proboscis muscles are predicted to be involved in proboscis positioning (such as reaching), while the other eight are predicted to be involved in pumping food through the pharynx.
evaluation: Claims C12-C13 represent predictions based on anatomical analysis of muscle insertion sites, supported by citations to prior work on pharyngeal pumping (Flood et al. 2013; Manzo et al. 2012; Tissot et al. 1998). These predictions are subsequently tested and validated through behavioral experiments described later in the manuscript.

result: The proboscis anatomy consists of two main segments (rostrum and haustellum) that pivot around distinct joints, with the rostrum having flexible unsclerotized cuticle supported by internal rigid cuticular structures. During feeding, food is sucked through the labella, pumped through the pharynx in the haustellum and rostrum, and enters the esophagus which passes through the brain.
evaluation: Claims C14-C24 describe proboscis anatomy and mechanics, supported by both prior work (Miller 1950, cited in C14-C16) and new imaging data shown in Figures 1 and Videos 1, 3, 4. The gluing experiments (C23-C24) provide direct experimental evidence for the location and function of the two joints.

result: The proboscis demonstrates directed reaching capability to ethologically relevant targets in different locations (ventral for feeding, anterior for courtship), making coordinated use of the head, rostrum, and haustellum. The haustellum shows independent control and adjusts its angle based on target position, with reaching guided by taste and proprioception rather than vision.
evaluation: Claims C27-C36 are supported by quantitative behavioral measurements shown in Figure 2 and Videos 5-8. Statistical analyses (Figure 2E-O) demonstrate significant differences in joint angles between feeding and courtship contexts, and the haustellum shows mean differences across target positions (C33). The gluing experiments (C35) and infrared filming design (C36) provide strong evidence for the conclusions.

result: A total of 16 proboscis muscles were identified in the mature adult fly through 3D segmentation, with other muscles present at eclosion that subsequently degenerate.
evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by detailed anatomical analysis shown in Figure 3A and Video 10. C38 is supported by citation to Miller 1950. The muscle count and nomenclature are documented in Table 1 and used consistently throughout the manuscript.

result: A final collection of 17 split GAL4 lines was selected from 389 combinations, with most targeting a single motor neuron type (exceptions: one line targets both mn11V and 12D, three lines target mn3). These lines show good reproducibility and are sparse in the CNS outside of proboscis motor neurons.
evaluation: Claims C39-C43 are well-documented in Table 1 and Figure 4 with Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The screening process and selection criteria are described in the Methods, and reproducibility data are provided in Table 1. The exceptions noted (C40-C41) are clearly documented.

result: All boutons on relevant muscles were completely occupied by labeled motor neurons (with noted exceptions for muscle 3 and mn10), demonstrating that the collection includes every primary motor neuron of the proboscis, with single motor neurons branching to many or all fibers of a muscle.
evaluation: Claims C44-C46 are supported by synaptic marker (nc82) staining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and documented in Table 1. The completeness argument (C45) is logical given the complete occupancy of synaptic sites. The exceptions for muscle 3 and mn10 are clearly explained in the text and Methods.

result: Motor neuron dendritic arbors (except salivary mn13) fall into two partially overlapping regions (dorsal and ventral) in the SEZ, with dorsal arbors generally corresponding to pharyngeal motor neurons and ventral arbors to non-pharyngeal motor neurons. This organization correlates with soma location and nerve exit routes.
evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are supported by anatomical analysis shown in Figure 5B and documented in Table 1. The correlation between dendritic location, muscle insertion site, soma location, and nerve routing is clearly demonstrated. Citation to Hartenstein et al. 2018 for nerve nomenclature is appropriate.

result: Computational registration reveals spatial relationships between motor neurons and other feeding-related neurons: sweet taste inputs avoid ventral motor neuron arbors and pass through circular gaps occupied by eye mechanosensory inputs; bitter taste inputs do not directly overlap retractor motor neurons; Hugin neurons are near mn1 and mn13; and Fdg command-like neurons show little overlap with motor neurons, suggesting additional interneuron layers.
evaluation: Claims C51-C61 are supported by computational registration data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 12. The spatial relationships are clearly visualized, and appropriate citations are provided for prior work (Gordon and Scott 2009; Hampel et al. 2017; Dethier 1976; Melcher and Pankratz 2005; Flood et al. 2013). The inference about additional interneuron layers (C61) is reasonable given the lack of direct overlap.

result: Eight muscles are associated with the pharynx (compared to three previously known): muscle 13 inserts at the salivary duct junction and is predicted to control salivation, while seven others insert on the pharynx wall. Sequential contraction of these seven muscles is predicted to create a traveling dilation that moves food through the proboscis, with peristaltic action taking over in the esophagus.
evaluation: Claims C62-C67 are supported by detailed anatomical observations shown in Figures 6A and 6—figure supplement 2, with comparison to prior work (Flood et al. 2013; Manzo et al. 2012; Tissot et al. 1998). The functional predictions (C63, C66, C67) are reasonable inferences based on muscle arrangement and insertion sites, though they remain to be tested experimentally.

result: Eight muscles do not insert on the pharynx and are therefore candidates for proboscis positioning.
evaluation: Claim C68 is supported by anatomical observations shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1. This prediction is subsequently validated through behavioral experiments testing each of these eight muscles.

result: Muscle 9 (mn9) is a rostrum protractor with wider effects: activation elicits extension of both rostrum and haustellum from rest but not during feeding; silencing does not affect rest position but prevents movement of both rostrum and haustellum during feeding, demonstrating both activation and silencing phenotypes at both joints.
evaluation: Claims C69-C75 are well-supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, and Video 14. Both CsChrimson activation and tetanus toxin silencing experiments show consistent phenotypes. The coupling between rostrum and haustellum movements is clearly demonstrated, though the mechanism remains to be fully explained.

result: Muscle 1 (mn1) is a retractor located in the rostrum with additional effects on the haustellum: activation retracts the proboscis beyond rest position (affecting rostrum but not haustellum from rest, but affecting both from extended position); silencing impairs proboscis retraction at rest.
evaluation: Claims C76-C79 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D, and Video 15. Both activation and silencing experiments show consistent retractor phenotypes, with context-dependent effects on the haustellum.

result: Muscles 2D and 2V are accessory rostrum retractors with distinct roles: mn2V activation causes rostrum retraction from rest while mn2D activation causes retraction from extended position; silencing mn2V causes small impairment at rest. These retractor muscles are not required for proboscis extension, only for retraction.
evaluation: Claims C80-C85 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B,D,G,I-J. The distinct roles of 2D and 2V (C80-C81) are clearly demonstrated. The lack of silencing phenotypes for some conditions (C82) and the conclusion about redundancy are reasonable. The conclusion that retractors are not required for extension (C85) is well-supported by the silencing data.

result: A biomechanical model explains rostrum movement: muscle 9 causes protraction by pulling on the free dorsal arm of an internal apodeme, swinging it ventrally; muscles 1, 2D, and 2V cause retraction by inserting on cuticle near the apodeme's ventral end. This model is supported by decreased muscle length and sarcomere spacing in the retracted state.
evaluation: Claims C86-C89 integrate anatomical observations (Figure 7P-Q, Video 16) with behavioral results to propose a coherent biomechanical model. The sarcomere spacing measurements (C88) provide direct evidence for muscle contraction states. The model is consistent with all experimental observations.

result: The haustellum can move independently of the rostrum. Muscle 4 (mn4) is responsible for haustellum extension, showing both activation and silencing phenotypes specific to the haustellum without affecting the rostrum. Silencing mn4 virtually abolishes haustellum extension during feeding, suggesting it may be the only muscle required for this movement.
evaluation: Claims C90-C95 are well-supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A-J, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-B, and Video 17. The independence of haustellum movement (C90) is demonstrated in Figure 2M-O and Video 4. Both activation and silencing experiments for mn4 show consistent, specific phenotypes for haustellum extension.

result: Muscle 3 (m3) controls haustellum flexion. Three split GAL4 lines targeting different parts of m3 (mn3M&1, mn3M&7, mn3L) all triggered haustellum flexion during feeding, with the phenotype attributable to m3 rather than contaminating cell types (mn1 or mn7). Silencing experiments showed impaired proboscis retraction at rest.
evaluation: Claims C96-C102 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A-F,M-N, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C-D, and Video 18. The use of multiple lines with different contaminating cell types (C97-C98, C100-C101) provides strong evidence that m3 is responsible for the observed phenotypes. The logic of comparing lines with and without contaminating neurons is sound.

result: A biomechanical model explains haustellum movement based on rotation of a Y-shaped apodeme: muscle 4 inserts on the free dorsal arm causing extension; muscle 3 crosses the joint causing flexion (possibly aided by muscle 2V inserting on the anterior arm). Sarcomere spacing measurements support these muscle actions in different haustellum positions.
evaluation: Claims C103-C110 integrate anatomical observations (Figure 8O-P) with behavioral results to propose a coherent biomechanical model. The sarcomere spacing measurements (C109-C110) provide direct evidence for muscle contraction states. The model is consistent with all experimental observations, though the role of 2V (C106) remains somewhat uncertain.

result: Muscles 6 and 7 insert on the labella and control labellar movements: muscle 6 shows both activation and silencing phenotypes for labellar extension; muscle 7 shows activation and silencing phenotypes for labellar abduction (opening). These are the only muscles showing labellar phenotypes.
evaluation: Claims C111-C115 are supported by anatomical observations (Figures 6B and 9A-C) and experimental data (Figure 9F-I, Videos 19-20). The inference that mn7's effect on extension is a side effect of abduction (C114) is reasonable given the lack of silencing phenotype for extension.

result: All eight muscles predicted to be involved in proboscis positioning based on insertion sites indeed showed positioning phenotypes: six control reaching movements (muscles 1, 2D, 2V, 3, 4, 9) and two control the labella (muscles 6, 7). Most findings were previously unknown or differed from previous work.
evaluation: Claims C116-C118 summarize the comprehensive behavioral characterization of all eight positioning muscles. The validation of anatomical predictions through behavioral experiments is a major strength. Comparison with prior work (Schwarz et al. 2017) is documented in Table 3.

result: This work provides the first comprehensive, genetically reproducible control of every primary motor neuron type for an appendage. The neurons are considered primary excitatory motor neurons based on their morphology, which differs from known modulatory and inhibitory motor neurons.
evaluation: Claims C119-C121 are supported by comparison with prior work (Baek and Mann 2009; Brierley et al. 2012; Maniates-Selvin et al. 2020; Rajashekhar and Singh 1994; Schwarz et al. 2017; Trimarchi and Schneiderman 1994; Rivlin et al. 2004; Wolf 2014). The classification as primary excitatory motor neurons is reasonable based on the anatomical and functional evidence presented.

result: Unexpected complexity was discovered in rostrum motor neuron phenotypes: both mn9 and mn1 showed effects on the haustellum despite being located near the rostrum. These may represent biomechanical coupling, where forcing movement of one body part causes movement of another, or afferent feedback leading to activation of other motor neurons. Similar biomechanical properties are known in insect legs during locomotion.
evaluation: Claims C122-C126 describe observed phenomena (C122) and offer speculative explanations (C123-C125) supported by analogy to known mechanisms in other insects (C126, citing Ache and Matheson 2013; Jindrich and Full 2002). The speculation is clearly labeled as such and is reasonable given the observations.

result: Combining activation, silencing, and insertion site data allows derivation of muscle roles that differ from previous work based mainly on activation. Several muscles are innervated by only one or two primary motor neurons, which may control slow and fast twitch fibers. This numerical simplicity presents an experimental advantage for circuit studies.
evaluation: Claims C127-C130 discuss methodological advantages and interpretations. C127 is supported by comparison with Schwarz et al. 2017 (Table 3). C128 is an observation from the anatomical analysis. C129 is speculation (clearly labeled) supported by analogy to known mechanisms (Azevedo et al. 2019). C130 is a reasonable inference about experimental advantages.

result: The proboscis has a varied repertoire of movements in feeding and courtship. Activation and inactivation experiments support a model of separable control, enabling articulated movements that allow flexibility.
evaluation: Claims C131-C132 are supported by citations (Manzo et al. 2012; McKellar et al. 2019) and by the comprehensive experimental results presented throughout the manuscript. The model of separable control (C132) is well-supported by the individual motor neuron manipulation experiments.

result: Proboscis reaching in flies could present a new model for understanding the neural circuit basis of goal-directed movement. Drosophila offers advantages including rich behavior, a smaller nervous system, powerful genetic tools, and an ongoing whole-brain synaptic connectome project.
evaluation: Claims C133-C138 place the work in broader context. C133-C135 cite appropriate prior work on reaching in various organisms (Parker 1974; Bower et al. 1970; Gutnick et al. 2011; Peterson 1934). C136 is a reasonable proposal based on the work presented. C137 is general knowledge about Drosophila. C138 cites the connectome project (Zheng et al. 2017).
